claims.text: The proposed intervention is to coat all exposed tungsten surfaces before W–Cu composite consolidation.
Magnetron sputtering can produce a uniform coating on reinforcing-particle surfaces prior to composite consolidation.
A 100–200 nm Mo or refractory high-entropy-alloy coating would function as a high-thermal-conductivity diffusion barrier in W–Cu.
Untreated W–Cu composites undergo W/Cu interfacial phase separation and void formation under the stated heat-flux and irradiation conditions.
The coating creates a deliberately engineered nanometer-scale interfacial layer between W and Cu.
An interfacial layer can have a graded or multilayer structure with compositionally distinct regions.
The engineered layer prevents or mitigates W–Cu interdiffusion that would otherwise cause phase separation and void nucleation.
The coating reduces W/Cu interfacial energy.
The coating suppresses interdiffusion between tungsten and copper during thermal cycling and irradiation.
The coating mitigates intermetallic or void-phase formation by relaxing local stresses, including stresses caused by thermal-expansion mismatch.
A continuous or graded W/coating/Cu transition supports more efficient phonon and electron transport.
Coating reinforcement-particle surfaces can improve interfacial bonding relative to an uncoated composite.
The coated W–Cu composite will retain a more homogeneous interface with fewer voids and phase-segregated regions than untreated W–Cu.
The coated W–Cu composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity under service conditions than the untreated composite.
Heat fluxes of 10–20 MW/m² and irradiation at 180–350 °C represent relevant service conditions for the proposed fusion joint.
The intervention may cease to be effective if radiation degrades the coating or if coating thickness is not adequately controlled.
